documentation.range: This species ranges discontinuously from Colombia to Argentina in South America. It occurs in all mainland countries in South America except Ecuador and Chile. This species generally is found at elevations between sea level and 2,000 m asl, but there is an isolated record in Boyacá, Colombia, at 2,100 m (J.R. Caicedo pers. comm. 2013) and another from Venezuela at 2,800 m (Campbell and Lamar 2004).
documentation.population: It is a common species. No significant declines have been reported, although in Uruguay its distribution has been reduced significantly and at present is restricted to the northern part of the country (Carreira et al. 2005).
documentation.habitats: This is a mainly terrestrial species, but in Brazil it has been observed in arboreal situations (Dayrell et al. 2010). It inhabits a broad range of habitats, ranging from dry sparsely vegetated stony areas or desert, to savanna and grasslands (M. Martins, pers. comm., 2010). It feeds almost exclusively on mammals (mainly rodents), eating lizards only rarely (Leynaud and Bucher 1999, Campbell and Lamar 2004, M. Martins pers. comm. 2010, G. Rivas and J.R. Caicedo pers. comm. 2013).
documentation.threats: It is hunted and persecuted by farmers, but on a range-wide scale no major threats are known.
documentation.measures: The subspecies Crotalus durissus terrificus is a priority species for conservation in Uruguay (Carreira and Estrades 2013). In places its distribution coincides with protected areas. No further conservation measures are required.
documentation.use_trade: It is used locally in traditional medicine for cancer treatment in the eastern llanos of Colombia.
documentation.rationale: Crotalus durissus has been assessed as Least Concern in view of its very wide distribution and its tolerance of a broad range of habitats. No specific threats have been reported, and this species probably is not undergoing significant population declines.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: The taxonomic rearrangement of Campbell and Lamar (2004) (based on morphology) was corroborated by the molecular data of Wuster et al. (2005), confining Crotalus durissus (previously understood to range throughout the Neotropics) to South America (M. Martins, pers. comm. 2010). Rivas et al. (2012) propose recognizing the current subspecies Crotalus d. vegrandis from the lowlands of Maturín and Anzoátegui (northeastern Venezuela) as a full species based only on size and colour pattern. This scheme is adopted by the Reptile Database as of November 2018 (Uetz 2018), however, other works do not (Campbell and Lamar 2004, Wuster et al. 2005) and the recognition of this species would warrant more evidence than a smaller size and a peculiar colour pattern.
